name: IcePanel
tagline: Collaborative C4 model diagramming for software architecture, with drill-down levels and a shared object model.

pricing.basis: per editor per month, annual and monthly tiers
pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: The interesting part of IcePanel is not the boxes and arrows, it is that objects live in one model and appear across every C4 level, so renaming a service once fixes every diagram. That is a data model plus an editor, and an agent can get you a credible local version: a JSON model, a React Flow canvas per level, drill-down, tags, and dependency links. Where it falls apart is everything around the model: multiplayer editing, diagram versioning and diffs, shareable read-only links for stakeholders who will never install anything, and the polish that makes non-engineers actually look at the thing. If you are one architect who wants a source of truth in Git, the DIY build is genuinely fine, and Structurizr DSL or Mermaid already covers a lot of it. If the point is getting twelve people across three teams to agree on a picture, you are buying the collaboration layer, not the renderer.
coreLoopDIY: A local model-driven architecture editor where systems, containers and components live in one JSON file and render as linked, drillable C4 diagrams.
requirements: a Git repo if you want history
whatYouLose: Real-time multiplayer editing and comment threads on diagram objects
Versioned diagram history with visual diffs between revisions
Clean read-only share links for stakeholders who will not run a dev server
Auto-layout that does not look like a spilled bowl of arrows
Integrations and import paths (Confluence, Slack, Terraform/cloud discovery, Draw.io imports)
moatNotes: Architecture diagrams are a social artifact. The tool wins by being the place everyone already looks, which is a hard thing to self-host into existence.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because architecture documentation dies the moment it becomes one person's side project. Teams pay so that the diagram is hosted somewhere permanent, editable by people who do not write code, commentable by the people who have opinions, and versioned so that last quarter's picture still exists. A local model-driven editor solves the modeling problem for the person who built it and solves nothing for anyone else, which is exactly the failure mode that made people buy a tool in the first place.
notes: The renderer is a weekend; the habit of a whole team keeping one diagram current is not.
prompt:
Build a local, single-user C4 architecture modeling tool. No accounts, no cloud, no telemetry.

Stack (do not deviate):
- Vite + React + TypeScript
- React Flow for the canvas
- Zustand for state
- Tailwind for styling
- Model persisted as a single JSON file on disk via a tiny Express server (GET /model, PUT /model), served alongside Vite in dev

Data model:
- One flat object registry: id, type (person | system | container | component), name, description, technology, tags[], parentId
- One flat relationship registry: id, sourceId, targetId, label, technology
- Diagrams are derived, not stored as duplicates: a diagram is (level, focusObjectId) and renders the children of that object plus any external objects it talks to
- Renaming or editing an object updates it everywhere, that is the entire point

UI:
- Left panel: tree of the model (system > container > component), click to open that object's diagram
- Center: React Flow canvas, drag to set node positions (persist positions per diagram in the JSON), double-click a node to drill into its child diagram, breadcrumb trail at the top to navigate back up
- Right panel: inspector for the selected object or relationship, editable fields, tag chips with colors
- Toolbar: add object, add relationship (click source then target), delete, tag filter, export current diagram as SVG and PNG

In scope: the shared model, drill-down levels, tag filtering, manual layout, SVG/PNG export, import from a Structurizr-style DSL subset if it is cheap to do.
Out of scope: multiplayer, comments, auth, versioning UI, auto-layout, cloud hosting, integrations.

Seed the model file with a small realistic example (a payments platform with 3 containers and 6 components) so the app is not empty on first run.
Any config in .env. Ship a README with run instructions and a note that the JSON file is the source of truth and should be committed to Git.
